newsitem.title: FRANCE: Defendants pass the buck at Tapie soccer trial.
newsitem.headline: Defendants pass the buck at Tapie soccer trial.

text.p: Fallen French soccer tycoon Bernard Tapie and his co-defendants passed the buck on Tuesday over the disappearance of 100 million francs ($17 million) from his former European champion club Marseille.
One by one, Tapie and the former top officials of the 1993 European champions denied responsibility for spending decisions or said they had only followed others' advice or obeyed orders.

Tapie, 54, serving an eight-month jail sentence for rigging a soccer match, told the court it was not his job as chairman to check if all the club's dealings were legally clean and denied direct involvement in the day-to-day management.
"When the chairman is shown a document, it's not up to him to know whether the company or the payment involved are within the rules. Otherwise there's no point in hiring staff," he said.
"I set the menu and the others did the cooking," Tapie said.

The rags-to-riches businessman-turned-politician, who was briefly a cabinet minister in a Socialist-led government in 1992-93, faces a five-year sentence if convicted on charges of swindling, misusing corporate funds and falsifying documents.
Other defendants insisted they acted on Tapie's orders.
"Tapie used to say 'I want that player'. He fixed the transfer costs and the club officials did their best to negotiate," former finance manager Alain Laroche said.
"I acted on the directives of Bernard Tapie. He knew we used middle-men and impresarios and that we gave 'loans' to players," he said.
Jean-Pierre Bernes, once Tapie's right-hand man, told the court he had no financial training or competence.
"I signed bills and contracts, but I didn't check whether it was according to the rules," he said.
Elie Fellous, ex-manager of Tapie's business empire and the club's former finance director, insisted he had only a symbolic function at the club and never dealt with its business dealings.
Michel Hidalgo, a former Marseille sporting director and French national soccer coach, also rejected all responsibility for financial irregularities.

The trial, expected to last three weeks, could shed light on alleged soccer corruption after Bernes promised "revelations". He has accused Tapie of spending five to six million francs ($850,000 to $1 million) a year on rigging French league and European cup games.
